newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Anti-nuclear protesters hurl firebombs in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Anti-nuclear protesters hurl firebombs in Taiwan.

text.p: Anti-nuclear protesters stormed a police line and fire-bombed a police jeep outside Taiwan's parliament on Friday as tempers flared hours before a crucial vote on the fate of a stonewalled fourth nuclear power station.

Militant activists hurled petrol bombs from a truck that crashed through a razor-wire barricade a few hundred meters (yards) from parliament and the presidential palace, the state-funded Central News Agency quoted police as saying.
A police jeep was torched and state television showed police dousing the flames.

Parts of Taipei's government district had been sealed off to control a final day of emotional pro- and anti-nuclear protests as parliament debated whether to uphold its cancellation of the US$4.1 billion needed to complete the unfinished fourth plant.
The cabinet has appealed the cancellation and a vote was expected late on Friday, with a two-thirds majority by opponents needed to make the controversial decision stand.

Friday's protests were raucous but peaceful until late morning when the truck ploughed into the barricade and 20 to 30 activists swinging banners mounted on sticks jumped out to clash with helmeted police armed with shields and clubs.
At least two demonstrators were detained, police said.
One police officer was hit by the protest truck and a local reporter was injured in the melee, police said. Both were taken to hospital for treatment of minor injuries.
Tensions have flared all week as anti-nuclear activists and parties opposed to the ruling Nationalist Party's nuclear policy have joined up to pressure parliament to vote down the project.
Parliament humiliated the government in May by cancelling funding, but state utility Taiwan Power has pushed ahead and the cabinet lodged a formal appeal, necessitating Friday's vote.
The Nationalists hold a slim 51 percent parliamentary majority and analysts have been reluctant to say whether they were likely to prevail in the showdown.
Hanging in the balance, among other things, was U.S. giant General Electric's US$1.8 billion contract to supply the light-water plant's twin reactors and generators.

Turning to increasingly militant measures, lawmakers from the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party tried to kill the project on Tuesday by physically preventing Premier Lien Chan from entering parliament to defend the cabinet's appeal.

Lien, who assailed the strong-arm tactics as a "dark day for democracy", has left nothing to chance and took the case for nuclear power directly to the public on Thursday with a live television appeal.
"We cannot have such important national projects being stopped every two or three days," Lien said.

He said Taiwan must diversify and widen its energy sources to ensure stable power supplies for its economic development. He dismissed environmental criticisms, saying a state-of-the-art nuclear plant was far cleaner than those burning carbon fuels.
Suggesting a possible compromise, Lien hinted strongly that Taipei would not seek to build further nuclear plants.
Taiwan Power already has sunk US$220 million into the 2,700-megawatt nuclear station outside Taipei.
